answers.question: 311 noise complaints in San Francisco rose over 60% in the year to mid-2026. Does that mean the city actually got dramatically louder?
answers.answer:
Not necessarily — a ~60–70% rise in 311 noise complaints (from ~11,000 to ~18,000 all categories, ~6,200 to ~7,700 excluding a catch-all category) shows *reporting* went way up, but that doesn’t directly prove the city actually got dramatically noisier. ([311info.com](https://311info.com/city/san_francisco/noise/?utm_source=openai))

Here’s why more complaints don’t equal a louder city:

• Easier reporting tools: SF upgraded its 311 app (and introduced tools like SolveSF), making it simpler to submit complaints — that tends to increase counts even without actual change in noise levels. ([sfchronicle.com](https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/311-wrapped-data-21279833.php?utm_source=openai))  
• Awareness & expectation shifts: As people grow more sensitive to noise (especially with more remote work, or living full time at home), or they see more coverage about noise issues, they’re likelier to file reports.  
• Super-users & repeat reports: A small number of people might complain a lot (even for the same recurring noise), skewing totals. For example, protests at a particular intersection have caused many complaints clustered in place/time. ([sfchronicle.com](https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/protest-noise-complaints-22325742.php?utm_source=openai))  
• Changes in definitions/app categories: The "catch-all" noise category here was inflated by a March 2026 app change, meaning part of the jump is statistical, not environmental. ([sfchronicle.com](https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/311-wrapped-data-21279833.php?utm_source=openai))

In short: Yes, there’s a strong case something has shifted — in either perception, reporting behavior, or possibly noise — but we don’t have conclusive evidence that ambient noise levels (actual loudness) have jumped with the same magnitude. answers.question: Police incident counts in Mission, San Francisco, rose this past year. Should I read that as the area getting more dangerous (as of mid-2026)?
answers.answer:
Not necessarily — the data suggests more “activity” by the police, but *fewer* incidents reported by victims, which muddies the picture of what’s actually happening. Here’s how to interpret the three metrics for the Mission:

- Crime_incidents rose ~4.1% (12,449 vs. 11,954) in the past 12 months. ([cde.ucr.cjis.gov](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/resources/reports/Reported%20Crimes%20in%20the%20Nation%202024%20FAQs.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
- Crime_victim_reported dropped ~20.5% (4,883 vs. 6,144). ([cde.ucr.cjis.gov](https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/resources/reports/Reported%20Crimes%20in%20the%20Nation%202024%20FAQs.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
- Crime_enforcement jumped ~72% (4,558 vs. 2,645), meaning police are initiating many more operations—warrants, sweeps, drug actions, etc. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R46668?utm_source=openai))  

Because fewer crimes are being reported by victims while enforcement is much more active, it’s not clear that the area is more dangerous. Possible explanations include:

- Victims feeling less trust in reporting (or less willingness to do so),  
- An increase in police-detected or enforcement-related incidents rather than spontaneous crime,  
- Or crimes being dealt with in ways that don't require victim reporting.  

So: incident counts alone *don’t* mean “more danger.” If you want, I can dig into trends in violent vs petty crime, or types of victim-reported crime, to better assess risk.

answers.question: The city's business registry shows 1431 closures in Financial District/South Beach, San Francisco, over the past year. Is the registry a reliable real-time count of business closures?
answers.answer:
No — the SF business registry’s count of closures (e.g. “business locations with a registry end date”) is *not* a reliable real-time indicator of business closures. Here’s why:

• Back-filling delays: End dates are often added well after a business has actually closed. The dataset includes “end dates … frequently backfilled late,” so recent months especially tend to understate closures. ([data.sfgov.org](https://data.sfgov.org/Economy-and-Community/Registered-Business-Locations-San-Francisco/g8m3-pdis/data?utm_source=openai))  
• “Administratively Closed” nuance: Some locations are marked “Administratively Closed” simply because they haven’t communicated with the city for three years—not necessarily because they recently shut down. ([data.sfgov.org](https://data.sfgov.org/Economy-and-Community/Registered-Business-Locations-San-Francisco/g8m3-pdis/data?utm_source=openai))  

So the registry gives a useful historical snapshot and high-level trends, but if you want *current* closure activity — say, most recent few months — it’s missing many closures until they're officially recorded.

answers.question: San Francisco assessed property values rose only about 2% last year. Does that mean market prices were roughly flat?
answers.answer:
No — a ~2% rise in **assessed** values *does not* mean market prices were flat. Because of Proposition 13, assessed values are capped at about 2% per year unless a property is sold or improved. ([sfassessor.org](https://www.sfassessor.org/sites/default/files/press-releases/Prop-13-Fact-sheet.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Here’s what that implies in San Francisco:

- If your property hasn’t sold or had major renovations, its assessed value is largely being dragged up by the inflation limit (usually ~2%), independent of what people are paying.  
- Market price changes — especially large ones, upward or downward — only show up in the assessed roll when there’s a sale (or construction-based reset). So market prices could easily have changed a lot more (or declined) without affecting the assessed values.  
- Recent data backs this up: while assessed values in SF rose just 1–2% in recent years, market indicators show that many homes **have declined** in value, though some segments (single-family homes, certain neighborhoods) have seen increases. ([sfchronicle.com](https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/property-tax-county-sf-20769394.php?utm_source=openai))

So, the ~2% assessed value growth is mostly a structural result of the tax law, not a reliable gauge of what homes are really selling for. If you want a clearer picture, look at recent sales data (e.g. MLS, Redfin, Zillow) in your neighborhood.
